newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Polls open in test-case Nigerian election.
newsitem.headline: Polls open in test-case Nigerian election.

text.p: The streets of Nigeria's main cities were deserted on Saturday as polls opened in local elections seen as a test of the military's commitment to return the vast Afrian nation to democracy.
Authorities ordered all public and private transport to stay off the road for the polling period from 8 a.m. (0700 GMT) to 4 p.m (1500 GMT).

Voting started on time but slowly in Nigeria's commercial capital Lagos, which has been at the forefront of opposition to military rule since the army aborted an earlier democracy programme nearly four years ago.

"I am here to vote because I want democracy to come back so the economy will be better," said Benjamin Otobo, the first voter in the queue at St Peter's Church polling station in the commercial district of Lagos.

The poll to elect chairmen and councillors to more than 770 town halls is the first multi-party ballot since General Sani Abacha seized power in November 1993. Voting is by secret ballot with all five registered political parties fielding candidates.
The last time Nigerians voted to end the army's long stranglehold on power ended in fiasco. The military abruptly scrapped the June 1993 presidential poll as a winner emerged.
Abacha seized power in the confusion that ensued, but Nigeria plunged further into crisis after he jailed the presumed winner of the election, southern businessman Moshood Abiola.
Police mobilised in Lagos after authorities warned they would deal ruthlessly with anyone causing trouble at polling centres. There were no immediate reports of any incidents in Lagos or elsewhere.
Residents of the inland capital Abuja said polling started there on schedule.
